idiom_name: atomic CAS loop over a shared FIFO (linked nodes or a bounded ring) plus a reclamation scheme
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep one atomic word per endpoint (head and tail pointers, or push/pop tickets), read it into a local copy, attempt a compare-and-swap of the published state, and retry when the CAS fails; publish the payload with release semantics before the CAS and observe it with acquire semantics after. For a bounded ring, give every slot a sequence word so producers and consumers each claim a position without a shared lock, and let full/empty be reported (false/null) rather than blocking. A linked-node design additionally needs a rule for when a removed node may be freed - garbage collection, hazard pointers, epochs/RCU, a type-stable pool, or tagged double-width CAS - because a node still referenced by a stalled thread must not be recycled. In most languages a library queue replaces the classic structure; write it by hand only when the platform has no equivalent or a hard real-time constraint demands a specific layout.
code_sketch:
loop:
    state = load(head, acquire)
    next  = state.node.next
    if CAS(head, state, next, acq_rel):        # claim and consume
        return state.node.value
    # CAS lost: reload and retry - no lock, no blocking
# publish side: write payload, then release-store the node into the link
pitfalls: A CAS loop alone is not enough: without a tag or counter in the same word, ABA silently corrupts the structure — a freed node's address is reused and the CAS succeeds on the wrong object.
Reclamation is the part that bites: a popped node freed while another thread still holds a pointer to it cannot be caught by ordinary testing; use hazard pointers, RCU epochs, or a GC.
Relaxed ordering everywhere is a data race in disguise — publication needs release semantics and the claim needs acquire semantics; defaulting to seq_cst is safe until profiling says otherwise.
False sharing on head/tail words: if head and tail share a cache line, each enqueue and dequeue invalidates the other's line, destroying throughput even though the algorithm is lock-free.

Spurious CAS failures under high contention: a thread can livelock retrying if multiple others are updating the same word; exponential back-off or pause instructions (x86 pause, ARM yield) break the feedback loop.
Compiler optimizations defeating lock-free code: without compiler barriers or proper atomic operations, the compiler can reorder or cache reads/writes in ways that break the algorithm's invariants.

x86 TSO vs ARM/POWER ordering differences: code correct on x86 (which has a strong memory model) may silently break on ARM or POWER where relaxed loads can be reordered; always specify explicit memory orders.

Wrong move: Treat lock-free as a per-thread latency bound -> Y fails because lock-free guarantees system-wide progress, not bounded steps for every operation -> instead document lock-free versus wait-free guarantees and measure tail latency under preemption and contention.

Wrong move: Free or recycle a removed node immediately after dequeue unlinks it -> Y fails because a stalled thread can still hold the old pointer, causing ABA or use-after-free -> instead use hazard pointers, epochs/RCU, garbage collection, or type-stable storage.

Wrong move: Assume epoch-reclamation batches are free -> Y fails because large batch frees can create allocator contention and latency spikes -> instead measure reclamation with the target allocator and amortize frees or tune the batch size.
